content: Sleep disorders are frequently observed in individuals with chronic kidney disease (CKD). Various strategies are employed in clinical practice to enhance sleep quality, including relaxation techniques, physical exercise, acupressure, and pharmacological treatments. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and potential adverse effects of interventions aimed at improving sleep quality in adults and children with CKD, including those with end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) undergoing dialysis or kidney transplantation. A comprehensive search was conducted in the Cochrane Kidney and Transplant Register of Studies up to October 8, 2018. This database includes studies identified through searches of CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, conference proceedings, the International Clinical Trials Register (ICTRP) Search Portal, and ClinicalTrials.gov. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-randomized RCTs that reported outcomes related to sleep quality were included. Two authors independently screened the studies, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias using the Cochrane tool. The certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Treatment effects were calculated as risk ratios (RR) for dichotomous outcomes or mean differences (MD) or standardized mean differences (SMD) for continuous outcomes. A total of 67 studies involving 3,427 participants met the inclusion criteria, with 36 studies (2,239 participants) included in meta-analyses. The follow-up period for clinical outcomes ranged from 0.3 to 52.8 weeks, with a median of 5 weeks. Interventions assessed included relaxation techniques, exercise, acupressure, cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), educational interventions, benzodiazepines, dopaminergic agonists, telephone support, melatonin, reflexology, light therapy, various forms of peritoneal dialysis, music therapy, aromatherapy, and massage. However, many studies had incomplete reporting of key methodological details, leading to an uncertain risk of bias. The evidence for relaxation techniques was of very low certainty, and their effects on sleep quality, sleep duration, health-related quality of life (HRQoL), depression, anxiety, and fatigue were uncertain. These studies were not designed to assess the impact of relaxation techniques on sleep onset latency or hospitalization. Exercise demonstrated uncertain effects on sleep quality (SMD -1.10, 95% CI -2.26 to 0.05; I² = 90%; 5 studies, 165 participants; very low certainty evidence). However, exercise likely reduced depression (MD -9.05, 95% CI -13.72 to -4.39; I² = 0%; 2 studies, 46 participants; moderate certainty evidence) and fatigue (SMD -0.68, 95% CI -1.07 to -0.29; I² = 0%; 2 studies, 107 participants; moderate certainty evidence). Acupressure had uncertain effects on sleep quality as measured by the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) (MD -1.27, 95% CI -2.13 to -0.40; I² = 89%; 6 studies, 367 participants; very low certainty evidence). However, acupressure likely slightly improved sleep onset latency (MD -0.59, 95% CI -0.92 to -0.27; I² = 0%; 3 studies, 173 participants; moderate certainty evidence) and sleep duration (MD -0.60, 95% CI -1.12 to -0.09; I² = 68%; 3 studies, 173 participants; moderate certainty evidence). The effects of acupressure on sleep disturbances were uncertain due to very low certainty evidence (MD -0.49, 95% CI -1.16 to 0.19; I² = 97%). Acupressure likely reduced fatigue (MD -1.07, 95% CI -1.67 to -0.48; I² = 0%; 2 studies, 137 participants; moderate certainty evidence). However, its effects on depression were uncertain (MD -3.65, 95% CI -7.63 to 0.33; I² = 27%; 2 studies, 137 participants; very low certainty evidence). No studies were designed to evaluate the impact of acupressure on HRQoL, anxiety, or hospitalization. When compared to sham acupressure, it was uncertain whether acupressure improved sleep quality (PSQI scale 0-21) due to very low certainty evidence (MD -2.25, 95% CI -6.33 to 1.82; I² = 96%; 2 studies, 129 participants). However, total sleep time may have been improved (SMD -0.34, 95% CI -0.73 to 0.04; I² = 0%; 2 studies, 107 participants; low certainty evidence). No studies specifically examined the efficacy of interventions for sleep-disordered breathing in CKD patients. Additionally, no studies reported treatment effects for children. The adverse effects of the therapies were highly uncertain. In conclusion, the evidence base for interventions aimed at improving sleep quality and related outcomes in adults and children with CKD is limited. Relaxation techniques and exercise had uncertain effects on sleep outcomes. Acupressure may improve sleep latency and duration, but these findings are based on a small number of studies and were not confirmed in trials using sham acupressure as a control. Given the very low certainty of the evidence, future research is likely to alter the current understanding. Considering the importance of symptom management for patients, caregivers, and clinicians, further studies on sleep interventions in CKD populations should be prioritized.
